summary: Acebrophylline is a combination molecule joining ambroxol, a mucolytic/secretolytic agent, with theophylline-7-acetic acid, a xanthine bronchodilator. It is used for airway diseases featuring bronchospasm and viscous secretions, including COPD, asthma, and acute/chronic bronchitis, providing both bronchodilation and improved mucus clearance. It carries theophylline/xanthine-class cautions (cardiac, CNS/seizure, and CYP1A2-related drug interactions). It is marketed in countries such as Italy, South Korea, and India and is not FDA-approved.
indications: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) with bronchospasm and hypersecretion
Other airway conditions with bronchospasm and viscid mucus (e.g. bronchiectasis, emphysema)

dosage.n: Standard adult capsule/tablet strength is 100 mg
Continue as prescribed; reassess periodically and adjust to response/tolerability

admin: Swallow capsule/tablet whole with water, preferably after food
Maintain a regular twice-daily morning and evening schedule
Ensure adequate hydration to aid mucus clearance
Review cardiac, seizure, and concomitant medication history before starting
Avoid combining with other theophylline/xanthine products to prevent toxicity
moa: The ambroxol moiety reduces sputum viscosity by stimulating serous gland secretion, breaking down acid mucopolysaccharide fibers, and promoting surfactant and mucociliary transport, easing expectoration. The theophylline-7-acetic acid moiety acts as a xanthine bronchodilator, inhibiting phosphodiesterase to raise intracellular cyclic AMP and antagonizing adenosine receptors, relaxing bronchial smooth muscle and exerting anti-inflammatory effects. Acebrophylline also reduces inflammatory mediator release and may downregulate phospholipase A2 activity, combining secretolytic and bronchodilator actions.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to acebrophylline, ambroxol, or xanthines

preg: Adequate human data in pregnancy are insufficient. Because of the theophylline-related component, avoid during pregnancy unless the benefit clearly outweighs the risk and under specialist supervision.
lact: Xanthines are excreted in breast milk and may cause irritability or other effects in the infant; data for acebrophylline are insufficient. Breastfeeding is generally not recommended during treatment, or treatment should be withheld.
renal: No formal adjustment scheme is established; xanthine and metabolite accumulation can occur, so use with caution and monitoring in significant renal impairment, with dose reduction as clinically indicated.
hepatic: Xanthine clearance is reduced in hepatic impairment, increasing toxicity risk; use with caution, consider dose reduction, and monitor in moderate-to-severe hepatic impairment.

major: CYP1A2 inhibitors (fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin and other fluoroquinolones, cimetidine) - raise xanthine levels/toxicity
Ephedrine/sympathomimetics - increased CNS and cardiac stimulation
moderate: CYP1A2 inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, smoking) - reduce xanthine levels/efficacy
Allopurinol, oral contraceptives, propranolol - may increase xanthine levels
minor: Antibiotics altering gut flora may marginally affect levels
Caffeine and xanthine-containing foods - additive stimulant effect
interactions.food: Take after food to reduce gastric irritation; large changes in dietary xanthine intake may affect tolerability
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; alcohol may increase xanthine levels and worsen GI and CNS adverse effects
interactions.diagnostics: Xanthine component may interfere with certain assays and can affect adenosine/dipyridamole stress testing; relevant if theophylline levels are measured

rare: Severe cutaneous reactions (reported with ambroxol, e.g. SJS/TEN-spectrum)
Hypokalemia and metabolic disturbance with high xanthine exposure
emergency: Status epilepticus / seizures from xanthine toxicity
Anaphylaxis / severe cutaneous reaction with airway compromise

monitoring: Heart rate and rhythm, especially in cardiac patients
CNS symptoms (tremor, agitation, seizures) suggesting xanthine toxicity
Interacting drugs and, where applicable, theophylline/xanthine effects
counsel: Take twice daily after food with water
Report palpitations, severe tremor, seizures, or marked restlessness promptly
Avoid alcohol and large amounts of caffeine while on treatment
Tell your clinician about heart problems, seizures, ulcers, and all other medicines (especially certain antibiotics)
Stay well hydrated to help clear mucus; report any skin rash or blistering immediately
pk: Bronchodilator effect within ~1-2 hours of oral dosing
Peak plasma concentration approximately 1-2 hours after oral dose
Xanthine component elimination half-life roughly 5-8 hours (variable)
Store below 25-30°C in a dry place, protect from light and moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved; record pending clinical review. Marketed in countries such as Italy, South Korea, and India.
Combines ambroxol (mucolytic/secretolytic, also boosts surfactant) with a theophylline-acetic-acid xanthine bronchodilator in one molecule
Apply theophylline-class precautions: narrow therapeutic margin, CYP1A2-mediated interactions (fluoroquinolones, fluvoxamine, smoking), and cardiac/seizure risk
Useful where both bronchospasm and viscid secretions coexist (e.g. COPD with productive cough)
Smoking induces xanthine metabolism and can lower efficacy; cessation may raise levels and toxicity risk
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered, unless it is almost time for the next dose; do not double up. Resume the regular twice-daily schedule.
overdose: Overdose reflects xanthine toxicity: nausea/vomiting, agitation, tremor, tachyarrhythmias, hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, and seizures, which can be life-threatening. Management is supportive—cardiac and electrolyte monitoring, activated charcoal (including multiple-dose for the xanthine), correction of hypokalemia, benzodiazepines for seizures, and beta-blockade or other agents for arrhythmias; consider charcoal hemoperfusion/hemodialysis in severe poisoning. No specific antidote.
